overview.title: Rare features, spurious correlations, and the noise-channel experiment
overview.section: 5.1 Generalization: The goal of machine learning
overview.main_topic: The third source of overfitting: rare or meaningless features that correlate with targets by chance, and the setup of an MNIST experiment that adds 784 noise or zero columns.
overview.central_idea: When a feature value is rare, or its association with the target is a statistical fluke, a model will still use it, learning a spurious correlation that does not hold for new data. Adding pure white-noise features to MNIST, which carries no information, is enough to provoke this.
overview.importance: Spurious correlations are described as 'one of the most common sources of overfitting'. The experiment set up here (results on p.166) shows the effect cleanly, and it motivates feature selection.
learning_objectives: Explain spurious correlation using the orange-tabby and cherimoya examples.
Understand why even a feature occurring 100 times can produce a fluke correlation (54% vs. 46%).
Read and explain Listing 5.1: flattening MNIST and concatenating 784 noise or zero columns.
Predict why noise columns hurt generalization while zero columns don't, though neither adds information.
prerequisites: NumPy arrays, reshape and concatenate along an axis.
Text classification by word features (IMDB, chapter 4).

summary:
This page introduces the third cause of overfitting named on p.162: **rare features and spurious correlations**.

It opens with a human analogy: if you had only ever met two orange tabby cats and both were antisocial, you might conclude that orange tabbies are antisocial. That's overfitting; exposure to more cats would show that color doesn't predict character.

Models do the same. In sentiment classification, if the word **"cherimoya"** (an Andean fruit; a footnote quotes Mark Twain calling it "the most delicious fruit known to men") appears in only one training text and that text is negative, a poorly regularized model may give the word a large negative weight and label every future cherimoya-mentioning text negative.

Rarity in the sense of a couple of occurrences isn't required. A word occurring in **100 samples**, positive 54% of the time and negative 46%, may show a difference that is a **complete statistical fluke**, yet the model will likely learn to use it. The authors call this "one of the most common sources of overfitting."

Then comes a **striking experiment**: take MNIST, flatten each image to 784 values, and build two new training sets of 1,568 columns, one by appending **784 white-noise columns** and one by appending **784 all-zero columns** (Listing 5.1). Neither addition changes the information content of the data; a human classifier wouldn't be affected at all. The page ends by announcing that the chapter 2 model will be trained on both sets (Listing 5.2, p.165), with the outcome shown in figure 5.6 (p.166).

paragraphs.excerpt: If you’ve only ever seen two orange tabby cats in your life,
paragraphs.what_it_says: Seeing only two orange tabbies, both antisocial, might lead you to infer orange tabbies are antisocial; that's overfitting, and seeing more varied cats would teach you that color is not well correlated with character.
paragraphs.what_it_means: With two samples, any feature they share (color) looks perfectly predictive of any property they share (temperament). The 'rule' is a coincidence of the tiny sample, and it is corrected only by more, more varied data.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It frames spurious correlation as a sampling problem: the fewer examples support a feature value, the more likely its apparent effect is accidental.

terminology.meaning: An association between a feature and a target that exists in the sample by chance but not in the underlying population.

connections: p.172: the book later stresses that denser coverage of the input space (more data) is the best fix for poor generalization.

paragraphs.excerpt: Likewise, machine learning models trained on datasets that include rare feature
paragraphs.what_it_says: Models trained on data with rare feature values are highly susceptible to overfitting. If 'cherimoya' appears in only one training text, which is negative, a poorly regularized sentiment model may weight it heavily and classify any cherimoya text as negative, although there is nothing negative about cherimoyas.
paragraphs.what_it_means: In a bag-of-words model each word has its own weight. A word seen once can have its weight pushed freely to fit that one example, since no other example constrains it. The gradient for that weight only ever 'sees' the one negative review, so the weight drifts towards strongly negative.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Large vocabularies contain thousands of such rare words (the long tail), so this is a pervasive risk in text models and a reason to restrict or regularize features.
paragraphs.technical_idea: For a rare feature j, the loss gradient with respect to w_j is nonzero only on the samples where feature j is active. With one such sample, minimizing training loss pushes w_j in one direction without limit unless regularization (e.g. an L2 penalty) pulls it back.

terminology.meaning: A model with little constraint on its weights, free to fit idiosyncratic features.
A feature (e.g. a word) that is active in very few training samples.

connections: p.130: IMDB sentiment classification in chapter 4 uses exactly this kind of word-presence feature.

paragraphs.excerpt: Importantly, a feature value doesn’t need to occur only a couple
paragraphs.what_it_says: Spurious correlations don't require extreme rarity: a word in 100 samples that is positive 54% of the time and negative 46% may show a difference that is pure fluke, yet the model will probably learn to use it. This is one of the most common sources of overfitting.
paragraphs.what_it_means: With n = 100 and a truly neutral word (50/50), the sample proportion has a standard deviation of about 5 percentage points, so 54% is well within ordinary chance variation. The model, however, sees only the training statistics and treats the 8-point gap as signal.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It shows that spurious correlations are not an edge case of rare words; they affect many moderately common features, which together can noticeably degrade generalization.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: the binomial standard error is sqrt(p(1-p)/n) = sqrt(0.25/100) = 0.05, so a 54% observation is 0.8 standard errors from 50%, nowhere near statistical significance.

terminology.meaning: A pattern produced by random sampling variation rather than a real effect.

connections: p.166: feature selection by a usefulness score such as mutual information is proposed as a remedy.

paragraphs.excerpt: Here’s a striking example. Take MNIST. Create a new training set
paragraphs.what_it_says: Build two modified MNIST training sets: one with 784 white-noise dimensions concatenated to the 784 pixel dimensions (half the data is noise), and one with 784 all-zero dimensions. Neither changes the information content; human accuracy would be unaffected.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This is a controlled experiment. Both datasets contain exactly the same useful information. The only difference is whether the added columns vary randomly (noise, which can correlate with labels by chance) or are constant (zeros, which can't correlate with anything). Any accuracy gap must therefore come from the model fitting chance correlations in the noise.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It isolates spurious correlation as the cause of degraded generalization, ruling out an information loss explanation.
paragraphs.technical_idea: An all-zero input column contributes nothing to a Dense layer's output (0 · w = 0) and its weights receive zero gradient, so it is completely inert. A noise column produces nonzero gradients that let the model fit random fluctuations.

terminology.meaning: Independent random values; here uniform in [0, 1) from np.random.random.
What the inputs reveal about the target; unchanged by appending independent noise or constants.

connections: p.165: Listing 5.2 trains the same model on both datasets.
p.166: figure 5.6 shows the noise version reaching about one percentage point lower validation accuracy.

paragraphs.excerpt: Now, let’s train the model from chapter 2 on both of these
paragraphs.what_it_says: Transition: the chapter 2 model will now be trained on both training sets.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The model is the 512-unit ReLU Dense layer followed by a 10-way softmax used for MNIST in chapter 2, redefined in Listing 5.2 on the next page.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Using the same, familiar model on both datasets keeps the comparison fair.

concepts.name: Spurious correlation
concepts.definition: An association between a feature and the target that appears in the training sample by chance but doesn't hold in general.
concepts.intuition: Two grumpy orange cats don't make orange cats grumpy.
concepts.technical: With finite n, the empirical correlation of an irrelevant feature with the target fluctuates around zero with spread about 1/sqrt(n); a flexible model exploits these fluctuations to reduce training loss.
concepts.significance: Called 'one of the most common sources of overfitting'; demonstrated with the MNIST noise-channel experiment.
concepts.example: 'cherimoya' appearing once in a negative review; a word 54% positive over 100 samples.
concepts.misconception: 'Only very rare features are dangerous.' The book's 100-sample example shows moderately common features can mislead too.

concepts.name: Rare features
concepts.definition: Feature values that occur in very few training samples.
concepts.intuition: A word that appears in one review can be assigned any meaning the model likes.
concepts.technical: Their weights are constrained by very few gradient contributions and can grow large to fit those few samples.
concepts.significance: Highly susceptible to overfitting, per the page.
concepts.misconception: Rare features aren't useless; they're unreliable, because their estimated effect has high variance.

concepts.name: Noise-channel experiment
concepts.definition: Appending 784 random columns (vs. 784 zero columns) to flattened MNIST to show that meaningless but varying features harm generalization.
concepts.intuition: Hand the model a second page of static; it will find 'patterns' in it.
concepts.technical: Training inputs go from shape (60000, 784) to (60000, 1568). Information content is unchanged; only the presence of fittable randomness differs between the two variants.
concepts.significance: A controlled demonstration of spurious correlations; results in figure 5.6 (p.166).
concepts.misconception: 'Zeros and noise are both meaningless, so they should behave the same.' Zeros are constant and inert; noise varies and can be (spuriously) fit.

math.title: How big is a chance fluctuation over 100 samples? (not in the book)
math.source_text: Not printed in the book; quantifies the page's '100 samples … 54% … 46%' example.

variables.meaning: True probability that a sample containing the word is positive (0.5 if the word is neutral).
Number of training samples containing the word (100).
Observed fraction of positive samples (0.54 in the book's example).
Standard error: typical size of the random deviation of \hat p from p.

math.operations: Binomial variance p(1-p) divided by n, then square root.
math.purpose: Shows that a 54/46 split is fully consistent with a neutral word.
math.interpretation: The observed 0.54 is only (0.54-0.50)/0.05 = 0.8 standard errors above 0.5; splits this lopsided or more occur by chance roughly 4 times in 10 for a neutral word.
math.intuition: Flip a fair coin 100 times: getting 54 heads is entirely ordinary.
math.numerical_example: With n = 100, values of $\hat p$ between 0.40 and 0.60 (±2 SE) are routine for a neutral word. Only with n ≈ 10,000 would SE shrink to 0.005, making 0.54 a genuine signal.

code.title: Adding white noise channels or all-zeros channels to MNIST
code.original_code:
from keras.datasets import mnist
import numpy as np

(train_images, train_labels), _ = mnist.load_data()
train_images = train_images.reshape((60000, 28 * 28))
train_images = train_images.astype("float32") / 255

train_images_with_noise_channels = np.concatenate(
    [train_images, np.random.random((len(train_images), 784))], axis=1
)

train_images_with_zeros_channels = np.concatenate(
    [train_images, np.zeros((len(train_images), 784))], axis=1
)
code.what_it_does: Loads MNIST training data, flattens each 28 × 28 image into 784 values scaled to [0, 1], and creates two augmented copies with 1,568 columns: one with 784 uniform random columns appended, one with 784 zero columns appended.

line_explanations.explanation: Import the MNIST loader from Keras and NumPy.
Load MNIST; keep training images and labels, discard the test split with `_`. train_images has shape (60000, 28, 28), dtype uint8.
Convert to float32 and divide by 255 so pixel values lie in [0, 1], the same preprocessing as chapter 2.
np.random.random((60000, 784)) draws uniform values in [0, 1), the same range as real pixels. np.concatenate(..., axis=1) glues them to the right of each row: shape (60000, 1568).
Same, but with an array of zeros: shape (60000, 1568), where the last 784 columns are always 0.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: the MNIST training split (downloaded on first use). Output: two NumPy arrays of shape (60000, 1568); train_labels (60000,) is reused unchanged for both.
code.algorithm: Flatten → normalize → horizontally concatenate either noise or zeros.
code.theory_link: Creates two datasets with identical information content; the only difference is whether the extra features can produce spurious correlations.

parameters.name: axis=1
parameters.role: Concatenate along the feature axis (columns), keeping 60,000 rows.
Number of added columns, equal to the number of real pixel features, so half the input is noise.

parameters.name: len(train_images)
parameters.role: Number of samples (60,000), so the added array has matching rows.

pitfalls: np.random.random and np.zeros return float64, so the concatenated arrays become float64 (double the memory of float32). Keras will cast to float32 when training.
Using axis=0 would stack new rows (samples) instead of new features and fail or silently produce the wrong shape.
The noise is regenerated every time this runs; set a seed (np.random.seed) for reproducible results.
Only the training split is modified; Listing 5.2 uses validation_split=0.2 from these same arrays, so validation data also contains the noise columns.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written sanity check (not from the book)
print(train_images.shape)                       # (60000, 784)
print(train_images_with_noise_channels.shape)   # (60000, 1568)
print(train_images_with_zeros_channels[:, 784:].max())  # 0.0
print(train_images_with_noise_channels.dtype)   # float64

deeper.title: Why zero columns are harmless but noise columns are not
deeper.body:
Beyond the book, for the first Dense layer $h = \operatorname{relu}(W x + b)$ with $x \in \mathbb{R}^{1568}$:

1. Split $W = [W_\text{pix}, W_\text{extra}]$, so $Wx = W_\text{pix}x_\text{pix} + W_\text{extra}x_\text{extra}$.
2. **Zeros**: $x_\text{extra}=0$, so $W_\text{extra}x_\text{extra}=0$ for every sample. The gradient of the loss with respect to $W_\text{extra}$ is (upstream gradient) × $x_\text{extra}^\top = 0$, so those weights never change. The model is mathematically identical to the plain 784-input model.
3. **Noise**: $x_\text{extra}$ differs per sample, so its gradient is nonzero. Over 48,000 training samples the network can find weight settings for which noise patterns happen to help predict specific training labels, i.e. it memorizes coincidences.
4. These coincidences don't recur in validation data (fresh noise), so the capacity spent on them is wasted and the noise adds variance to predictions, so validation accuracy drops (about 1 point, figure 5.6 on p.166).

deeper.title: Superstitions as spurious correlations
deeper.body: A footballer who scored twice while wearing the same socks decides the socks are lucky. Two observations, one shared feature, one shared outcome: the same structure as the two antisocial orange tabbies. More games would reveal the socks don't matter, just as more data dilutes the cherimoya effect.

deeper.title: Real-world spurious features
deeper.body: Note (not in the book): classic cases include image classifiers that learn to detect a watermark or a hospital-specific scanner tag instead of the pathology, or animal classifiers that rely on the background (snow for wolves). These are spurious correlations at scale, and they are harder to catch than white-noise channels because the shortcut feature also appears in the validation data.

visualizations.title: Shape flow in Listing 5.1
visualizations.why: Listing 5.1 flattens MNIST to (60000, 784) and concatenates 784 extra columns along axis 1; this traces the shapes.

misconceptions.claim: Adding irrelevant features can't hurt; the model will just learn to ignore them.
misconceptions.correction: If the features vary, the model will find chance correlations in them and use them; the experiment set up here demonstrates the cost (figure 5.6, p.166).

misconceptions.claim: A feature has to be very rare to cause a spurious correlation.
misconceptions.correction: The book's word with 100 occurrences and a 54/46 split shows a moderately common feature can mislead too.

misconceptions.claim: The noise dataset contains less information about the digits.
misconceptions.correction: It contains exactly the same information; the book stresses that the concatenation 'does not at all affect the information content of the data'.

takeaways: Rare or meaningless features let models learn spurious correlations, a top source of overfitting.
A word seen once (cherimoya) can receive a huge weight in a poorly regularized model.
Even 100 occurrences with a 54/46 split can be pure chance, and the model will still use it.
Listing 5.1 builds two 1,568-feature MNIST datasets: pixels plus 784 noise columns, or plus 784 zero columns.
Both have identical information content; any accuracy difference comes from fitting noise.

questions.question: Why does a poorly regularized sentiment model classify cherimoya texts as negative?
options: Cherimoya is a negative word in English
The only training text containing it was negative, so the model gave the word a large negative weight
The word is out of vocabulary
questions.answer: The only training text containing it was negative, so the model gave the word a large negative weight
questions.explanation: The page explains it as a rare-feature spurious correlation. The book notes there is 'nothing negative about the cherimoya'; out-of-vocabulary words would be ignored, not weighted; and the problem is precisely that the model doesn't ignore rare words.

questions.question: What are the shapes of train_images_with_noise_channels and train_images_with_zeros_channels?
questions.explanation: train_images is reshaped to (60000, 784); concatenating a (60000, 784) block along axis=1 doubles the feature dimension.

questions.question: Both added blocks carry zero information about the digit. Why might the noise block hurt validation accuracy while the zero block doesn't?
questions.answer: Zero columns are constant, contribute nothing to the Dense layer's output and get zero gradient. Noise columns vary per sample, so the model can fit chance correlations between noise patterns and labels, and those correlations don't hold on new data.
questions.explanation: This is the spurious-correlation mechanism the page describes; the result is shown on p.166.

questions.question: A neutral word appears in n = 100 training reviews. What is the standard error of the observed positive fraction, and how many standard errors from 50% is the book's 54%?
questions.explanation: This (AI-added) calculation shows that the 54/46 split is well within chance variation, which is why the book calls it a possible 'statistical fluke'.

questions.question: In Listing 5.1, what does axis=1 in np.concatenate do?
options: Adds 784 new feature columns to each sample
questions.answer: Adds 784 new feature columns to each sample
questions.explanation: axis=1 is the feature axis of a (samples, features) matrix. Adding samples would be axis=0; flattening is done by reshape; normalization by / 255.

questions.question: What lesson does the orange-tabby anecdote teach, and how is it corrected?
questions.answer: Generalizing from two cats that share a color and a temperament is overfitting to a tiny sample; meeting a wider variety of cats would show color doesn't correlate with character.
questions.explanation: The book's own conclusion: exposure to more varied data reveals the correlation to be spurious.

questions.question: Could you write Listing 5.1 from memory, including the correct shapes and axis?
questions.answer: Load MNIST, reshape to (60000, 784), cast to float32 and divide by 255, then np.concatenate([x, np.random.random((len(x), 784))], axis=1) and the same with np.zeros.
questions.explanation: Recreating it checks your grasp of the reshape/concatenate mechanics.
